description: Mangifera indica: an evergreen tropical fruit tree.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.description: The most important disease of mango: dark spots on young leaves, blackened flowers and rotting fruit.
diseases.causes: Spores from infected leaves, twigs and old flower stalks spread by rain splash; wet weather at flushing and flowering favours it.
symptoms: Small dark brown to black spots on young leaves, often with a yellow edge
Spots join; leaf tissue dries and may fall out
Black, withered flower panicles; sunken black spots on ripening fruit
diseases.effect: Leaf spotting, flower loss and fruit rot reduce the crop.
diseases.untreated: Repeated years of blossom blight can cut yields heavily.

steps.title: Remove spotted leaves, dead twigs and old flower stalks
steps.instruction: Pick off spotted leaves, dead twigs and old flower stalks when the plants are dry and take them away.
steps.rationale: Fewer spores are left to spread.

steps.title: Prune to open the canopy
steps.instruction: Thin the crown after harvest so it dries quickly.
steps.rationale: Spores need wet leaves and flowers.

steps.title: Protective spray
steps.instruction: Spray a registered fungicide at flushing and flowering on the label's schedule.
steps.rationale: Protects healthy growth; it cannot cure what is already infected.

prevention.title: Remove fallen leaves and dead wood
Watch flushes and flowers in wet weather

lifecycle: The fungus lives on leaves, twigs and old flower stalks.
Rain splashes spores onto new flushes and flowers.
Dark spots form on leaves; flowers blacken.
Fruit is infected and rots as it ripens.

diseases.name: Bacterial Canker (Black Spot)
diseases.description: A bacterial disease of mango leaves, twigs and fruit with raised, angular black spots.
diseases.causes: Bacteria survive in leaf and twig lesions and spread by wind-driven rain, especially through wounds.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked, angular spots limited by the veins
Spots turn raised, black and cracked, often with a yellow halo
Black, star-shaped cracks on fruit that ooze in wet weather
diseases.effect: Spotted leaves drop; fruit is blemished and may rot.
diseases.untreated: Severe outbreaks defoliate trees and spoil most fruit.

steps.title: Remove infected twigs and leaves
steps.instruction: Pick off infected twigs and leaves when the plants are dry and take them away.
steps.rationale: Fewer spores are left to spread.

steps.title: Plant windbreaks
steps.instruction: Shelter the orchard from strong wind.
steps.rationale: Wind-driven rain spreads the bacteria and wounds the leaves.

steps.title: Copper spray where advised
steps.instruction: Spray a registered copper product following the label.
steps.rationale: Protects new growth.

lifecycle: Bacteria survive in leaf and twig lesions.
Wind-driven rain carries them to new leaves.
Angular water-soaked spots turn black and raised.
Fruit gets cracked black spots.
sources: MangoLeafBD (Mendeley Data) class: Bacterial Canker, mango bacterial canker

diseases.name: Leaf-Cutting Weevil
diseases.description: A small weevil that lays eggs in young mango leaves and then cuts the leaves off near their base.
diseases.causes: Adult weevils are active on new, tender flushes; the females cut the leaves so the egg-bearing pieces fall to the ground.
symptoms: Young leaves cut straight across near the leaf base
Cut leaf pieces lying under the tree
Flushes left with only stubs of leaves
diseases.effect: New flushes lose their leaves, delaying growth.
diseases.untreated: Young trees in nurseries can be stripped of new leaves.

steps.title: Collect fallen leaf pieces
steps.instruction: Gather and destroy the cut leaf pieces under the tree.
steps.rationale: They hold the weevil's eggs and larvae.

steps.title: Watch new flushes
steps.instruction: Check tender flushes for weevils in the morning.
steps.rationale: Damage happens on young leaves.

steps.title: Control on severe attack
steps.instruction: Use a control registered locally, following the label.
steps.rationale: Protects the next flush.

lifecycle: Adults feed on tender new leaves.
Females lay eggs in the young leaves.
They cut the leaves near the base.
Larvae develop in the fallen pieces.
conditions: Fallen leaf pieces left under trees.

diseases.name: Die Back
diseases.description: A fungal disease that kills mango twigs and branches from the tip downward.
diseases.causes: The fungus enters through wounds and stressed tissue; drought, sun scald and damage favour it.
symptoms: Leaves at the shoot tips turn brown and dry, starting from the edges
Twigs die back from the tip; the bark darkens
Gum oozes from cracks in the bark
diseases.effect: Branches die and the crown thins.
diseases.untreated: Severe die back can kill large limbs or young trees.

steps.title: Prune out dead twigs
steps.instruction: Cut 10-15 cm below the dead part into healthy wood and remove the prunings.
steps.rationale: The fungus spreads down the twig.

steps.title: Seal and protect cuts
steps.instruction: Treat large cuts as advised locally.
steps.rationale: Wounds let the fungus in.

steps.title: Water and feed the tree
steps.instruction: Reduce drought stress.
steps.rationale: Stressed trees die back more.

lifecycle: The fungus lives on dead wood.
It enters through wounds and stressed twigs.
Shoot tips brown and dry.
The die back moves down the branch.
sources: MangoLeafBD (Mendeley Data) class: Die Back, mango die back

diseases.name: Gall Midge
diseases.description: Tiny flies whose larvae form small raised galls on mango leaves.
diseases.causes: Midges lay eggs in young leaves; each larva makes a small wart-like gall as it feeds.
symptoms: Many small raised, wart-like galls on the leaf, 3-4 mm
Galls dark brown to black, sometimes with a pale halo
Heavily galled leaves curl and drop early
diseases.effect: Galled leaves photosynthesise less and drop.
diseases.untreated: Heavy infestations weaken young trees and new flushes.

steps.title: Remove heavily galled leaves
steps.instruction: Pick off heavily galled leaves when the plants are dry and take them away.
steps.rationale: Removes larvae before they drop to pupate.

steps.title: Disturb the soil under the tree
steps.instruction: Rake or till the soil under the crown.
steps.rationale: Larvae pupate in the soil.

steps.title: Control on new flushes if severe
steps.instruction: Use a control registered locally, following the label.
steps.rationale: Protects the young leaves.

lifecycle: Midges lay eggs in young leaves.
Larvae feed inside, forming galls.
Mature larvae drop to the soil.
They pupate and emerge for the next flush.

diseases.name: Powdery Mildew
diseases.description: A fungal disease that coats mango flowers, young fruit and leaves with white powder.
diseases.causes: Spores blow on the wind; cool nights and dry, mild days at flowering favour it.
symptoms: White powdery patches on young leaves, often on the underside
Flower panicles covered in white powder, then brown and dry
Young fruit drops
diseases.effect: Flowers and young fruit drop, so the crop is small.
diseases.untreated: Severe attacks at flowering can wipe out the crop.

steps.title: Remove badly mildewed panicles and leaves
steps.instruction: Pick off badly mildewed panicles and leaves when the plants are dry and take them away.
steps.rationale: Fewer spores are left to spread.

steps.title: Open the canopy
steps.instruction: Prune for airflow and light.
steps.rationale: Shade and still air favour mildew.

steps.title: Protective spray
steps.instruction: Spray sulphur or another registered fungicide at flowering on the label's schedule.
steps.rationale: Protects healthy growth; it cannot cure what is already infected.

lifecycle: The fungus survives on old leaves.
Spores blow onto young leaves and flowers.
White powder covers them.
Flowers and young fruit drop.

diseases.name: Sooty Mould
diseases.pathogen: Capnodium and related sooty moulds (growing on insect honeydew)
diseases.description: A black, soot-like coating of fungi growing on the honeydew of sap-sucking insects.
diseases.causes: Mango hoppers, scale insects and mealybugs drop sticky honeydew on the leaves; sooty moulds grow on it.
symptoms: Black, papery or velvety coating on the upper leaf
The coating can be rubbed or peeled off
Sticky leaves; hoppers, scales or mealybugs nearby
diseases.effect: The coating shades the leaves and reduces photosynthesis.
diseases.untreated: Heavy coating weakens the tree and soils the fruit.

steps.title: Control the sap-sucking insects
steps.instruction: Deal with hoppers, scales or mealybugs as advised locally.
steps.rationale: No honeydew, no sooty mould.

steps.title: Wash the coating off
steps.instruction: Spray water (with a mild soap where advised) on badly coated leaves.
steps.rationale: Restores light to the leaves.

steps.title: Control ants
steps.instruction: Keep ants off the tree.
steps.rationale: Ants protect the insects that make honeydew.

lifecycle: Sap-sucking insects feed on the tree.
They drop sticky honeydew on the leaves.
Sooty moulds grow on the honeydew.
A black coating shades the leaves.
